title: Tongues of the machine
tagline: Every language is an argument about what programmers should have to think about. Sixty years of that argument, in the order it was made.

events.title: Fortran
events.summary: The first high-level language people actually adopted — because its compiler produced code fast enough to end the argument.
keyPoints: Formulas could be written as formulas instead of as register moves.
The team's real problem was credibility: assembly programmers had to believe the output was competitive.
It made the optimising compiler a necessity, not a luxury.
Still the language of record in high-performance numerical computing.
events.impact: Established that a language could be worth a layer of translation — the assumption every language since has inherited.

resources.label: Backus on the history of Fortran

events.title: Lisp
events.summary: A notation for symbolic expressions that turned out to be a language — and one where a program is just another piece of data.
keyPoints: Code and data share one representation, so programs can write programs.
Garbage collection appears here, because symbolic work makes manual freeing untenable.
Recursion, first-class functions, and the read-eval-print loop all arrive together.
`eval` was written to prove a point and turned out to be an interpreter.
events.impact: Most ideas that later feel new in mainstream languages — closures, dynamic typing, REPLs, macros, garbage collection — were in Lisp first, sometimes by thirty years.

events.title: ML
events.summary: Type inference and algebraic data types, invented to keep a theorem prover honest.

events.title: Scheme
events.summary: Lisp reduced to its core: lexical scope, proper tail calls, first-class continuations.

events.title: Haskell
events.summary: Purity and laziness as defaults, so effects have to be admitted in the type.

events.title: OCaml
events.summary: ML with objects and a compiler fast enough for industry to notice.

events.title: Clojure
events.summary: A Lisp on the JVM built around immutable data and explicit state.

events.title: COBOL
events.summary: Designed so that business people could read the program, on the theory that readable code outlives its author.
keyPoints: English-like syntax was a deliberate bet on maintenance over brevity.
Fixed-point decimal arithmetic, because money is not a float.
Record and file structure are first-class parts of the language.
The bet largely paid off: much of it is still running.
events.impact: Proved that legibility to non-authors is a real design axis — and produced the longest-lived production code in the industry.

events.title: ALGOL 60
events.summary: Barely used in production, and the ancestor of nearly everything — including the way we write down what a language even is.
keyPoints: Block structure and lexical scope: names mean something local.
Its report defined the language in BNF, so grammars became formal artefacts.
Recursion was specified deliberately, not discovered accidentally.
Hoare: "an improvement on nearly all of its successors."
events.impact: Every curly-brace language is an ALGOL descendant, and the ALGOL 60 report set the standard for what a language specification should look like.

resources.label: Report on the Algorithmic Language ALGOL 60

events.title: C
events.summary: Close enough to the machine to write an operating system, portable enough that the operating system could move.
keyPoints: The abstract machine is thin: what you write is close to what runs.
Rewriting UNIX in C in 1973 proved systems software need not be assembly.
Manual memory management is the price of that thinness, and the source of decades of vulnerabilities.
Its ABI is still the interoperability layer between every other language.
events.impact: Became the substrate. Operating systems, language runtimes, databases, and the calling convention that lets any two languages talk are all C-shaped.

resources.label: The Development of the C Language

events.title: C++
events.summary: Abstraction with no runtime cost you did not ask for — and a language that never removes anything.

events.title: Java
events.summary: A managed runtime as the portability layer, and garbage collection for the mainstream.

events.title: C#
events.summary: Java's shape with faster iteration — generics, LINQ, async/await arrive early.

events.title: Go
events.summary: Deliberately small, with concurrency as a language feature rather than a library.

events.title: Rust
events.summary: The memory-safety argument, settled at compile time instead of at runtime.

events.title: Smalltalk-80
events.byline: Alan Kay, Adele Goldberg & team, Xerox PARC
events.summary: Not a language so much as a whole running world, in which objects get things done by asking each other.
keyPoints: Everything is an object; the only operation is sending a message.
The environment is live — you edit a running system rather than restart one.
The class browser, the debugger, and the overlapping-window GUI shipped with it.
Kay's "object-oriented" meant messaging and late binding, not inheritance hierarchies.
events.impact: Gave the industry object-orientation, the modern IDE, and the desktop metaphor — then watched the first of those get adopted with the least of its original meaning.

resources.label: The Computer Revolution Hasn't Happened Yet

events.title: Python
events.summary: Optimised for the time a program spends being read, which turned out to be most of its life.
keyPoints: Indentation is syntax, so the layout cannot lie about the structure.
Batteries included: the standard library was the adoption strategy.
The C API made it the glue over fast native code — which became its second career.
The 2-to-3 migration is the industry's clearest lesson in the cost of a breaking change.
events.impact: Became the default language of scientific computing, data work, and machine learning — largely because it is comfortable to read and easy to wrap around something faster.

events.title: Java
events.summary: Sold as write-once-run-anywhere; its lasting contribution was making a managed runtime respectable.
keyPoints: The JVM, not the syntax, is the durable artefact — a dozen languages now target it.
Garbage collection at enterprise scale stopped being a research question.
JIT compilation showed that late binding need not mean slow.
Verbosity was a deliberate trade for tooling and large-team legibility.
events.impact: Set the template for the managed-runtime platform, and its JIT and GC research fed back into every runtime built since.

events.title: JavaScript
events.summary: Written in ten days to make web pages twitch, and now the only language every computer on earth can already run.
keyPoints: Prototypes and first-class functions came from Self and Scheme, under a Java-shaped syntax.
Its universal availability made it a compilation target for everything else.
The event loop made non-blocking I/O the default mental model for a generation.
Standardising it (ECMAScript) is how a rushed language was made repairable.
events.impact: The web's only native language, which means every alternative — TypeScript, Elm, WebAssembly's early story — is defined by its relationship to it.

resources.label: TypeScript
resources.note: Gradual types over the same runtime

events.title: Rust
events.summary: Argues that memory safety and manual control are not a trade-off, if the compiler is willing to be difficult about it.

media.alt: Ownership and lock motif for Rust

keyPoints: Ownership and borrowing move lifetime errors from runtime to compile time.
No garbage collector, and no use-after-free — the two were assumed to be a package deal.
"Fearless concurrency": data races are a type error rather than a debugging story.
The learning curve is the cost, and it is charged up front on purpose.
events.impact: Shifted the industry's default assumption about systems programming. Memory-safety mandates now name it explicitly, and both Linux and Windows have taken it into the kernel.
